fixes.explanation: No fire and no slipping away here. Eleazar and David stationed themselves in the middle of the field and defended it. Setting it on fire would be the opposite of defending it. They struck down the Philistines, and the LORD brought about a great victory.

Bethlehem it is. David said, "Oh, that someone would get me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!" The text says the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem at that time. Of all the wells to wish for, he picked one in a town with a Philistine garrison.

Hebron is a real place, but it's not the one David named. He said, "Oh, that someone would get me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!" The text says the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem at that time. So Bethlehem is the town to remember.

Jericho isn't in this story at all. David longed for water from "…the well near the gate of Bethlehem!" The text says the garrison of the Philistines was at Bethlehem at that time. So the town to remember is Bethlehem.

The text doesn't say anything about the troops getting it. It says David refused to drink the water, and instead he poured it out to the LORD. He said the Three had brought it at the risk of their lives (1 Chronicles 11:19). That's where the water went: out to the LORD.
Moab, friend. Benaiah son of Jehoiada, a man of valor from Kabzeel, struck down two champions of Moab. The text calls him a man of many exploits, and this is one of them.
Edom isn't the nation the text names. It says Benaiah struck down two champions of Moab. The verse is clear that these two champions came from Moab. Hold on to Moab for this one.

Ammon does show up in this list, because Zelek the Ammonite is one of the mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:39). But the two champions Benaiah struck down were from Moab, not Ammon. A name in the list can easily tag along into a different story. Keep Moab for Benaiah's champions.

He went down into the pit and killed it, and the text says it was a snowy day. Most people see a lion in a pit and stay on the top side, very politely. Benaiah went down. The text calls him a man of valor and a man of many exploits.
That's a sensible plan, but it's not what the text says. On a snowy day, Benaiah went down into a pit and killed a lion. The text has him going in after it.
Waiting for the lion to come up would be one way to do it, but that's not what the text says. On a snowy day, Benaiah went down into a pit and killed a lion. The text has him going down to it.

Exactly. The Egyptian's spear was like a weaver's beam, but Benaiah went against him with a club, snatched the spear from his hand, and killed the Egyptian with his own spear. The text says the Egyptian was a huge man, five cubits tall. I'd say a club against that spear is a bold way to show up.

The text doesn't mention any helpers in this scene. It says Benaiah went against the huge Egyptian, who had a spear like a weaver's beam, with a club. Then he snatched the spear from the Egyptian's hand and killed him with it. It also says Benaiah did not become one of the Three (1 Chronicles 11:25).

Guard is right. Benaiah did not become one of the Three, but the text says David appointed him over his guard. It also says he was most honored among the Thirty. The text puts those two facts side by side.
Vineyards are never mentioned in this passage. The text says David appointed Benaiah over his guard. That's the job the verse names, and it's the one to remember.
A treasury is a big job, but it isn't mentioned in this passage. The text says David appointed Benaiah over his guard. Guard is the job the verse gives him.
